> **If any of the IDs above are missing from the sprite that your style loads, the shield will fall back to “bare number only”.** The numbers themselves come from the `text-field` (glyphs) and are fine; the badge is the missing `icon-image`.
Below is a step-by-step guide to make those badges appear **without touching the style’s layer definitions**.
1. **The style’s `icon-image` expression** (e.g. `""{network}_{ref_length}""`) resolves to one of the IDs above.
2. The MapLibre runtime looks for that ID in the **sprite index** (`sprite.json`).
*If the ID is not present* → `styleimagemissing` fires, the console prints `Image ""<id>"" could not be loaded`, and the layer draws only the text part (the number).
So the problem is *missing sprite entries*, not a problem with the layer code.

## 3. Getting the badges without editing the style
You have three practical ways to make those IDs available:
### A. Point the style at a sprite sheet that already contains them
The easiest solution is to use the **official OSM Bright sprite** (or the OSM Liberty sprite) that ships with the OpenMapTiles style.
*Why this works* – Those sprite directories contain **all** the IDs listed in the table above.
* Do **not** use the `raw.githubusercontent.com` URLs in production (rate-limited, no SLA).
* If you already have a custom sprite (e.g. your own POI icons) you can keep it **and** add the OSM Bright sheet as a second sheet (see B).
### B. Add a second sprite sheet that only contains the shield badges
Since MapLibre GL JS ≥ 3.0 you can declare **multiple sprite sheets** in the style:
1. **Create a minimal sprite** that contains just the 13 (or 19 for Liberty) PNG badge images.
* Use `spritezero`, `spreet`, or the **Martin** web UI to turn a folder of PNGs into `sprite.png` + `sprite.json`.
* Name the PNG files exactly as the IDs above (`us-interstate_1.png`, `road_3.png`, …).
2. Host the two files (`sprite.png`, `sprite.json`) and the optional `@2x` versions on a domain you control (same-origin or CORS-enabled).
3. Add the sheet to the style as shown.
4. **Reference the sheet** in the layer’s `icon-image` **only if you need a prefix**.

* Because the existing style already uses the default sheet for its own icons, you **do not** have to change any `icon-image` values – the style will automatically resolve `us-interstate_2` against the *default* sheet **unless** you gave the OSM sheet the id `default`.
* The recommended pattern is to give the OSM sheet the id `default` and move your own sheet to a non-default id, e.g.:
Now all existing `icon-image` strings (including the shield IDs) resolve unchanged, and you can still use `my-icons:my-poi` for your own icons.
5. **Programmatic alternative** – after the style loads you can add the sheet from JavaScript:
This works even if the style’s `sprite` property is a single string; `addSprite` creates the second sheet at runtime.
### C. Register the missing badge images at runtime with `addImage`
If you cannot change the style’s `sprite` property (e.g. you are consuming a third-party style that you cannot edit) you can **inject the missing images yourself**:
*Pros* – No need to touch the style file.
*Cons* – Each badge is a separate HTTP request (unless you bundle them in a sprite and use `addSprite`). This is fine for a handful of images but not ideal for large custom sprite sets.

Below is a step-by-step guide, plus a few gotchas and debugging tips.
When a style’s `sprite` is a **single string**, MapLibre loads **one** PNG/JSON pair and builds a single image namespace.
All `icon-image` values are looked up **only** in that namespace.
If you later host a second sprite sheet somewhere else and simply set `icon-image: ""cafe""` (or any other name that exists only in your sheet), the lookup fails:
* The sprite JSON that was loaded does **not** contain the key `""cafe""`.
* The map therefore fires a `styleimagemissing` event and writes a single console warning:
* Because the warning is emitted only once per missing ID, you may not see it again after the first failure, which can look like “nothing logs an error”.
The fix is to give the map **more than one sprite namespace** and tell it which namespace to use for each icon.

Each entry is treated exactly like the old string form, *except* that the IDs become a **namespace prefix** for the images that live in that sheet.

* All other IDs **must be used as a prefix** (`<id>:<image-name>`).

anti-pattern — shield detection that compares symbol-placement as a string,skills/maplibre-sprites-icons/SKILL.md,"Reviewing my style-audit script. It flags a MapLibre symbol layer as a route shield when layer.layout['text-anchor'] === undefined and layer.layout['symbol-placement'] === 'point'. It is tagging plain place-name layers as shields and skipping real shield layers. Is the heuristic sound, and what should it key off instead?","## TL;DR
* **The current heuristic (`text-anchor` missing + `symbol-placement === ""point""`) is not reliable.**
* `text-anchor` is optional on *any* symbol layer that has no text (or that relies on the default “center”).
* Many point-based POI / place-name layers also have `symbol-placement: ""point""` and no `text-anchor`, so they will be mis-identified as shields.
* **A more robust “shield-detector” should look for the *signature* of a shield layer, not for the absence of a property.**
* Presence of an **icon-image expression that references a network-/ref-length placeholder** (`""{network}_{ref_length}""`, `""road_{ref_length}""`, `""default_{ref_length}""`, etc.).
* Presence of a **text-field that uses the `{ref}` placeholder** (or a similar expression that pulls the route number from the feature).
* Presence of **`icon-text-fit`** (usually `""both""` or `""width""`), which tells the style to stretch the badge to fit the route number.

* (Optional but helpful) a **`symbol-placement` that is a zoom-function / expression** that switches between `""point""` and `""line""` – most shield layers do this so the badge can appear on both point- and line-based features.
* (Optional) a **layer id or source-layer name that contains “shield”, “road-shield”, “transportation_name”, etc.** – this is a cheap “hint” you can use in addition to the structural checks.
Below is a deeper walk-through of why the original test fails, followed by a concrete implementation you can drop into a style-audit script.
## 1. Why `text-anchor === undefined && symbol-placement === ""point""` is a bad heuristic

column4: Why it’s not shield-specific

column3: Controls where the *text* is anchored relative to the icon. If a layer has **no text** (or relies on the default “center”), the property is omitted.
column4: Almost every point-based POI layer that only shows an icon (e.g., a café, a park) will have `text-anchor` missing. Shields *also* often omit it, but that omission is not exclusive to shields.

column3: Tells the renderer to place the symbol at a point geometry (or at a point derived from a line). It is the default for POI / place-name layers and for many shield layers that are rendered as points on low-zoom tiles.
column4: The default for *any* point-based symbol layer is `""point""`. Shields that appear on line features usually have a **zoom-function** that switches to `""line""` at higher zooms, but the low-zoom “point” branch still matches the test.

column1: Result: **high false-positive rate** (plain POI layers flagged as shields) and **high false-negative rate** (shield layers that use a zoom-function or that explicitly set `text-anchor: ""center""` are missed).
All OSM-derived shield styles (OSM Bright, OSM Liberty, OpenMapTiles, etc.) share a **two-part composition**:

1. **Badge (icon-image)** – a pre-drawn background that is *different* for each `ref_length` (or a stretchable badge). The `icon-image` value is **not a static literal**; it is an **expression** that interpolates the feature’s `network` and `ref_length` (or just `ref_length`).
2. **Route number (text-field)** – the actual road number, taken from the feature’s `ref` (or `ref:ref`). The `text-field` is also an expression that injects `{ref}`.
If **both** of those are present, you are almost certainly looking at a shield.
When a style uses a **single badge image** for *all* ref lengths, the badge entry in the sprite JSON contains `stretchX`/`stretchY` and `content`. The style then sets:
The presence of `icon-text-fit` (or `icon-text-fit` set to anything other than `""none""`) is a strong shield indicator because most POI layers never need text-fit.

Shield layers often need to appear **as points on low zooms** (when the road is not yet rendered as a line) and **as line-symbols on higher zooms**. The style therefore uses a **zoom-function** (or an expression) for `symbol-placement`:

If `symbol-placement` is a **plain string** (`""point""` or `""line""`), it does *not* rule out a shield, but a **zoom-function** is a *positive* clue that the layer is trying to handle both point- and line-based rendering – a pattern that POI layers rarely need.
* The presence of a **`network`** or **`ref_length`** property in the layer’s `filter` or `layout` (e.g., `""filter"": [""has"", ""ref""]`).
These are not required for correctness, but they help prune edge-cases when the expression-based checks are ambiguous.

column2: **Is the marker part of the style (i.e., collides with other symbols)?**
column3: No. A `Marker` lives in the DOM **above** the GL canvas, so it never participates in collision detection. If you need thousands of points that should collide with labels, use a **symbol layer** with a sprite instead.
